title: Banda Singh Bahadur
hookLine: an ascetic from the south meets Guru Gobind Singh at Nanded and becomes the Khalsa's commander

lines: A HERMIT WITH A SPECIAL SEAT.
cards: Nanded, on the banks of the Godavari river, deep in the south of India, 1708. A holy man lives in a hermitage there.
He has left the world behind: no family, no possessions, many followers, and a reputation for strange powers. People say visitors who sit on his special seat get tipped off it.
One day he comes home and finds a stranger sitting on that seat, completely at ease. The stranger is Guru Gobind Singh.

teach.b: The hermit's story, as tradition tells it, started far from Nanded. He was born in 1670 in the hills near Kashmir and named Lachhman Dev.
As a young man, the story goes, he went hunting and killed a doe, and watched her unborn young die with her.

It shook him so badly that he gave up the world and became a wandering ascetic, Madho Das, and ended up in the south, at Nanded. Guru Gobind Singh had come south too, after losing his sons and his city.
Tradition says Madho Das tried his powers on the Guru, and they did nothing. Shaken, he asked who this was. Then he said, in effect: I am your banda.
Banda means servant, one bound to another. He took amrit, and the name that stuck was Banda Singh. Later people added Bahadur, the brave.
Here's the turn. The Guru didn't ask Banda to go deeper into his hermitage.
He sent him out: to Punjab, where the Sikhs were being crushed and the killers of the Guru's young sons still held power.
Tradition says the Guru gave him five arrows from his own quiver, a flag, a drum, and a small band of Sikhs, with letters asking the Khalsa to rally behind him.
The Guru himself died at Nanded later that year. So the man who'd walked away from the world was sent straight back into it. For Sikhs, Banda's story is a picture of what a call can do.
Sometimes the service asked of you is the thing you'd left behind.

how: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur as the commander Guru Gobind Singh sent to lead the Khalsa in Punjab; the gurdwara at Nanded, Hazur Sahib, is one of the five takhts, marking where Guru Gobind Singh spent his last days.

o: a sweet rice dish cooked for weddings
a servant, one bound to another
a woven basket for carrying grain

games.q: who, where and what — tap the pairs.

s: Banda was born in the south of India
tradition says he was born near Kashmir and settled at Nanded as a hermit.
he called himself the Guru's banda.
the Guru told Banda to stay in his hermitage
he sent him out to Punjab with arrows, a flag, a drum and a band of Sikhs.

games.q: you're a hermit who left the world years ago. the Guru you've just accepted asks something of you. what?
o: go back out, to Punjab, and lead.
games.why: Guru Gobind Singh sent him out. the man who'd left the world was called back into it to serve.

practice: Think of a direction you've been walking in for a while, a habit, a job, a way of spending evenings or of treating someone, and ask it honestly: is this where I'm needed?
Picture a small change of direction, just one degree, toward someone who could use you: a call you've been avoiding, a skill you've kept to yourself. You don't have to act yet; just hold the picture.

wordCard.voice: Banda. A servant, one bound to another — the name the hermit Madho Das took when he pledged himself to Guru Gobind Singh and was sent to lead the Khalsa.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: banda, a servant, one bound to another; bahadur means brave.

carryVoice: Your line: called to serve. From hermit to servant, then sent out to lead. See you in Punjab tomorrow.

sources.ref: The meeting of Guru Gobind Singh and Madho Das at Nanded, 1708, as told in Sikh tradition
